stature.source: typical: the Gymnosperm Database 30-50 m, up to about 75; record: 78.94 m near the Rogue River, Oregon (2022); the largest living, the Mossy Creek Giant in Yosemite, is 71.6 m (Gymnosperm Database); read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-04), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a tall clear trunk with a few enormous horizontal limbs in the upper half, gaps between them, a flat or broken top; blue-green, darker than ponderosa

pole.note: a young tree: a narrow, regular cone of upswept branches on a smooth grey-brown trunk

old-growth.note: the giant: a long clear column of a trunk and, at the top, a few huge level arms reaching far out, heavy cones hanging from their ends, the top flat and ragged

description: The tallest and largest pine in the world, 30-60 m here, with a long straight column of a trunk, a crown of a few enormous horizontal limbs that reach far out and droop at the ends, and the longest cones of any conifer, 25-50 cm, hanging from their tips. It grows on the deeper soils of the mixed conifer forest of the west slope, about 1200-2400 m, scattered among white fir, incense cedar and ponderosa, its flat, lopsided top rising above them all.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen; the long cones hang from the limb ends like ornaments.
season_notes.spring: Pollen in May-June; new cones begin as small purple knobs.
season_notes.summer: The second-year cones grow long and green, pulling the limb tips down.
season_notes.fall: The great cones open in August-September and drop large winged seeds; the fallen cones litter the forest floor all year.

range.where: the mixed conifer forest of the west slope on deep soils: Crane Flat, Wawona, Hodgdon Meadow, the Hetch Hetchy road

notes: The silhouette is everything: young trees are narrow cones like other pines, but mature ones carry a handful of very long, nearly level limbs high on the trunk, so the crown is gappy, asymmetric and flat-topped, and the limb ends bend under the cones. The generator's ponderosa branching gives evenly spaced limbs; the crown profile, lobes and asymmetry here push it toward the open, one-sided form, but the few-huge-limbs architecture really needs a lower branch count and longer level-1 limbs (levels cannot be patched per index by the card). Cones 25-50 cm (Gymnosperm Database) are not drawn. Needles are short (5-10 cm), in fives, blue-green. White pine blister rust kills many. The sweet resin that gives the name is a field-guide line. Seeds are large and favoured by squirrels, chipmunks, jays and bears (the bear note is the drafter's knowledge). Central Sierra elevations are the drafter's knowledge.
